1.pericope_label: I determined not to come again in heaviness; and I wrote unto you with many tears

schools.summary: Begin by removing the chapter break, which is obviously wrong and interrupts the sequence of thought: the apostle is still explaining why he did not come, and the sentence should be read as continuing that explanation. Render the opening verb for myself, and note that he consulted his own feelings as well as theirs. Then raise the question the English hides. What is meant by again? Either he had already paid a second visit besides the one recorded in Acts, and that visit had been a sorrowful one, or, having had one joyful visit, he did not wish the second to be in grief. Either interpretation is possible as the Greek stands, and scholars disagree; there is no way to tell clearly, and it is a little odd that he did not plainly say so earlier if he had made such a visit. On the second verse, mark the particle that carries the paradox: it accepts the condition and springs the surprise, and the verb rendered make sorry is a causative matched by another causative meaning to make joyful. Explain the force of the connecting word, which lies below the surface. It might have been said that he had not seemed to mind giving pain when he wrote; his answer is that the man on whom the pain falls is thereby given the power of making him glad, so that the severity works out its own compensation. The abruptness of the question and the singular number show that the one great offender is before his eye. On the third verse, raise the harder question honestly. Is the tense the epistolary aorist, meaning this present letter? That is possible in itself, but the context and the seventh chapter make it improbable; and if it is not, we cannot say with certainty which letter is meant, since what follows can hardly apply to the first epistle and may point to a letter now lost. Add that the pronoun refers to nothing actually said, which shows how definitely certain passages of that letter stood stamped upon his memory. Then take the fourth verse as the answer to a charge. It had perhaps been said that severity cost him nothing; he replies that the letter was written out of pressure and constriction of heart, and through tears. Gloss the word for anguish as a holding together, a tightness or contraction of the heart under grief, a word used in the New Testament by only two writers and perhaps another instance of medical vocabulary. Then draw the lesson from the manner rather than the matter: it was not by sarcasm, nor by publishing the fault abroad, nor with any pleasure in rebuking, but by an affectionate letter written weeping. Admonition would always be done rightly if it were done with tears; the heart of an offender melts when the man who reproves him comes with tears; and it is worth saying how few who undertake to reprove ever do.

Fix the tense before anything else, for the whole sense of the delay hangs on it: the verb must be rendered as a pluperfect, I had determined, since he is assigning the reason for a delay that has already occurred and explaining what his intention had been beforehand. Say plainly what the earlier coming was. He had come once already by an epistle, and by that means had severely pained them; so long as they had not repented he was unwilling to come in person, lest he should be constrained to grieve them again, and he chose rather to give them longer time for repentance and amendment. Note also that the passage is still clearing him of the charge of levity and inconstancy, and softening what some had thought excessive severity in the former letter. On the second verse, take it as the proof of the statement just made. No one willingly occasions sorrow to himself; and the apostle has such a fellow-feeling with these people, such an agreement and connection of affection between him and them, that he cannot feel joyful unless he sees them happy. He goes further and calls them the source and authors of his joy, which they could not be if they were themselves sorrowful. Draw the pastoral rule out of that, and press it: if this disposition prevails in pastors, it will be the best restraint to keep them back from alarming with terrors the minds they ought rather to have encouraged by a cheerful affability, since from the want of it arises an excessive and morose harshness, so that we do not rejoice in the welfare of the Church as we ought. On the third verse, observe that he came the first time in sadness by a letter precisely so that they might not have to feel that severity when he was present; they have therefore no ground to complain of the sadness, in which he was consulting their welfare. Note too that he does not merely soften the keenness of that letter but says openly that his aim in writing was not to grieve them but to prove his attachment. On the fourth verse, weigh the temper from which reproof must come. Those who smile while others weep show their cruelty and are not to be borne; he declares that intensity of grief extorted from him everything he wrote. There are many noisy reprovers who, by declaiming or rather fulminating against vice, display a surprising ardour of zeal while remaining perfectly at ease in their own minds, as though they exercised throat and sides by way of sport. It is the part of a pious pastor to weep within himself before he calls upon others to weep, to feel tortured in silent musing before he shows any token of displeasure, and to keep within his own breast more grief than he causes to others. Let the tears themselves be defended, for they show a tenderness more heroic than the iron-hearted hardness of those who wished to seem devoid of feeling.

Take the passage as a continued explanation of a delay, and give the reason for it in one sentence: because of the scandals that were among them he could not have seen them comfortably, and he therefore determined not to see them at all until he had reason to believe those evils were put away. Then explain what a visit would have cost. Had he come and used his apostolic authority in inflicting punishment upon the transgressors, this would have been a common cause of distress; and though he might have expected the sound part of the church to be a comfort to him, yet as all would have been overwhelmed with trouble at the punishment of the offenders, he could not have rejoiced to see those whom he loved in distress. Put the second verse in the plainest possible terms, since its logic is simple once stated: he cannot be comforted himself until the offender's grief is removed, and it is the man he has grieved who must be the one to cheer him. On the third verse, say what the earlier letter was for. He had marked that matter particularly, earnestly desiring their reformation, so that if he came before it had taken place he must have come with a rod and inflicted punishment on the transgressors; and he assures them that he knows they wish his comfort as much as he wishes theirs, his joy being the joy of them all. Then meet the charge that lies behind the fourth verse. It is very likely that his enemies had represented him as a harsh, austere and authoritative man, better pleased with inflicting wounds than with healing them. He vindicates himself by solemnly asserting that this was the most painful part of his office, and that the writing of that first letter cost him much affliction and anguish of heart and many tears. Set the motive beside the pain: it was not so much that they might be grieved as that they might know, by his faithful admonition, his abundant love toward them. Let the whole of it be turned to use in the pulpit and in private dealing alike. A reproof given by a man who is manifestly grieved to give it will be received as a reproof from a man who enjoys giving it never can be; and where the reprover's own heart is untouched, the words, however true, will be read as authority asserting itself rather than as love at work.

State the reason for the change of plan simply, as the passage does: he did not come because he was unwilling to grieve them, or to be grieved by them. He had determined not to come in heaviness, which he must have done had he come and found scandal among them not duly dealt with; and that would have been cause of grief on both sides, since their sorrow or joy at meeting would have been mutual. If he had made them sorry, that would have been a sorrow to himself, for there would have been none left to make him glad. What he desired was a cheerful meeting, not one embittered by some unhappy occasion of disagreement. Then say that the former letter was written to the same end. He wrote so that he might not have sorrow from those of whom he ought to rejoice, and he wrote in confidence of their doing what was requisite, both for their benefit and for his comfort; and note that he was not disappointed of that expectation. Guard the motive of the letter as carefully as the motive of the delay: he did not design to grieve them, but to testify his love, and he wrote with much anguish and affliction in his own heart and with great affection toward them, writing with tears that they might know his abundant love. Draw two notes from that, and let them be pressed on anyone who has to reprove. First, that even in reproofs, admonitions, and acts of discipline, faithful ministers show their love; the severity is not the opposite of the affection but one of its instruments. Second, that needful censures, and the exercise of church discipline toward offenders, are a grief to tender-spirited ministers, and are administered with regret. He desired a cheerful meeting with them, and wrote in confidence that they would do what was to their benefit and his comfort, and would therefore be glad to remove every cause of disquiet from him. Close with the rule that covers every such case, and let it stand as the application: we should always give pain unwillingly, even when duty requires that it must be given.

5.pericope_label: Sufficient to such a man is this punishment; forgive him, and confirm your love

schools.summary: Warn the reader at once that the fifth verse is ambiguous, and that the ambiguity is not in the English only: the abrupt qualifying clause and the absence of authoritative punctuation leave the construction open. Three explanations are possible. The first: if any has caused grief, it is not the apostle alone whom he has grieved, but in part, to some extent, all of them, since the members of that church were really the greatest sufferers from a scandal which brought shame upon it. The second: he has not grieved the apostle except in part, that is, he is not the only offender, and the qualification is added so as not to press the charge against them all as though they were equally condemnable. The third combines the two. Prefer the first as the simplest and most natural; and in any case note that the pronoun stands first in the Greek and is therefore emphatic, me he has not grieved. Add that the parenthesis about not pressing too heavily interrupts the flow of ideas, and that the verb in it, to put a burden upon, is a late word which in the New Testament belongs to this writer only. Note also that the offender is never named, here or anywhere: he is a man, such a one, and it is not possible now to know who he was. On the sixth verse, render the noun censure or rebuke rather than punishment, since the Greek word is not the one used for punishment elsewhere; and take it as a late term meaning an adjudged penalty. Reconstruct what the censure had been: a meeting of the church, the man delivered over as the first letter directed, possibly some bodily suffering, and almost certainly excommunication and exclusion from religious and social fellowship. The apostle had clearly heard what it was and judged it enough. Then press the phrase rendered of many, which properly means by the majority, by the more; and draw the inference, that the decision had not been unanimous. Consider who the minority may have been, whether those who resented what looked like dictation, or the party of licence against whom the earlier letter argued. Others resist that reading and take the phrase for the whole assembled body, arguing that the words cannot naturally be made to describe a single bishop or a bench of elders, and pointing to the older renderings that give the majority, the greater number, or the whole body of your society. If the whole society is meant, it shows the way discipline was actually administered; but be candid that a single instance in the early churches does not by itself bind all later ones. On the seventh and eighth verses, note the change of tone as indignation passes into pity, and the strength of the language: what if he should be swallowed up, drunk down as in a great deep of sorrow? Suicide, madness and apostasy seem to float before the writer's mind as possible results. Render the last verb ratify or make valid, a legal term found only here and once in Galatians, and take it to require an act as formal and public as the rebuke had been: the man was to be re-admitted by a collective act of the church.

Take the fifth verse as an alleviation of the offence rather than an aggravation of it. The apostle says that he had grief in common with them, and that the occasion of it came from another quarter: we have been alike grieved, and another is to blame for it. Speak of that other mildly, as the text does, not affirming the thing but leaving it in suspense, and reading the conditional as concession rather than as doubt, since the incestuous person is plainly designed though he is not named. Prefer the reading that takes the sentence as one continuous whole, so that the meaning is, he has not so much grieved me as, in some measure, all of you, the qualification being added so as not to bear too hard upon him. Set aside the ingenious reading which makes the qualification mean a part of the saints only, on the ground that the church was divided; it is more ingenious than solid. Then, on the sixth verse, mark what the apostle is doing and why it matters. He now extends kindness to the man who had sinned more grievously than the rest, and on whose account his anger had been kindled against them all, because they had connived at the crime; and in showing indulgence even to one who deserved severer punishment, he gives them a striking proof how much he disliked excessive harshness. Say what the censure had been, that the man had been excommunicated by the apostle's direction, and that the church had been sharply reproved for having so long encouraged that unhappy man in his sin by their dissimulation and patient endurance; and note that this passage shows he had been brought to repentance after being admonished by the church. Then make the passage the rule it was meant to be, and observe it carefully, for it shows with what equity and clemency the discipline of the Church ought to be regulated, that there may not be undue severity. There is need of strictness, so that the wicked may not be made more daring by impunity, which is justly called an allurement to vice; but on the other hand, since a man who is chastised is in danger of becoming dispirited, moderation must be used, so that the Church stands ready to extend forgiveness as soon as she is satisfied of his penitence. Judge the ancient bishops by that rule and do not excuse them, but mark their error so that we may learn to avoid it. The apostle is satisfied with the repentance of the offender, that a reconciliation may take place; they, making no account of his repentance, issued canons of three years, of seven years, and in some cases of a whole lifetime, and by these they shut unhappy men out of the fellowship of the Church, so that the offender is either alienated the more or induced to practise hypocrisy. Even were the enactment more plausible in itself, this alone would condemn it, that it is at variance with the rule of the Holy Spirit which the Apostle here prescribes. Then state the end of excommunication exactly: that the offender, overpowered with a sense of his sin, may be humbled before God and the Church and may seek pardon with sincere confession of guilt. The man who has been brought to that is now more in need of consolation than of severe reproof; and if you continue to deal with him harshly, it will not be discipline but cruel domineering. Guard carefully against pressing men beyond that limit, for nothing is more dangerous than to give Satan a handle by which to tempt an offender to despair, and we furnish Satan with arms in every instance in which we leave without consolation those who are in earnest affected with a view of their sin.

Refer the qualifying phrase in the fifth verse to the people rather than to the degree of the grief, and say why. Only a part of them had given cause of grief, namely the transgressor and those who had taken his part; and it would therefore be unreasonable to load them all with the blame that attaches to that party alone. Read the sentence accordingly: he still rejoices over the greater part of them, and speaks as he does so as not to burden the whole body. Then, on the sixth verse, note first the manner and only afterwards the matter, for the manner is itself instructive. Observe with what remarkable tenderness this offender is treated: he is never once named, nor is his crime here so much as mentioned. Then say that the man had already suffered sufficiently, and that this is a proof of the apostle's parental tenderness toward a great transgressor. He had been disowned by the Church; he had deeply repented; and now the apostle pleads for him. On the phrase rendered of many, take it that not the rulers of the church only but the whole congregation acquiesced in the sentence, so that both the censure and the pardon are acts of the body. On the seventh verse, give the reason for haste. The punishment inflicted had answered the end for which it was inflicted, and there was real danger that if this poor culprit were not restored to the bosom of the Church his distress and anguish would destroy his life or drive him to despair. On the eighth, expound the word confirm as ratify, and make the practical demand plain: they do love him, notwithstanding the reproach he brought upon the Gospel, and it was because of their love to the Gospel's credit that they were obliged to cut him off; now that he has repented, they are to ratify that love by a public act of the Church, giving him the fullest proof of it by forgiving him and restoring him to his place. Let the hearer see the shape of the whole: a church that can punish but cannot restore has learned only half its duty, and the half it has not learned is the one on which a man's soul may hang.

Treat this passage as the principal occasion of the letter, and take it in order. First, the crime of that person had grieved the apostle in part; and he was grieved also with a part of them who, notwithstanding the scandal found among them, were puffed up and had not mourned. Yet he was unwilling to lay too heavy a charge upon the whole church, especially since they had cleared themselves in the matter by observing the directions formerly given them. Second, the punishment inflicted upon the offender was sufficient: the desired effect had been obtained, for the man was humbled, and they had shown the proof of their obedience. Third, they are therefore directed, with all speed, to restore him to their communion; and mark that this is expressed in three ways. They are besought to forgive him, that is, to release him from church censures, for they could not remit the guilt of an offence against God. They are to comfort him, for in many cases the comfort of penitents depends upon their reconciliation not only with God but with the men whom they have scandalised or injured. And they are to confirm their love to him, that is, to show that their reproofs and censures proceeded from love to his person as well as from hatred to his sin, and that their design was to reform and not to ruin him; or, if his fall had so weakened their love that they could not take the satisfaction in him they once did, then, now that he is recovered by repentance, they must renew and confirm it. Then set out the arguments used to persuade them, for the passage is a piece of reasoning and not merely an appeal. The case of the penitent called for it, since he was in danger of being swallowed up with overmuch sorrow: he was so sensible of his fault, and so much afflicted under his punishment, that he was in danger of falling into despair. Add the general rule that carries beyond this case, that when sorrow is excessive it does hurt, and that even sorrow for sin is too great when it unfits a man for other duties and drives him to despair.

debates.question: How is the qualifying clause but in part to be construed?

sides.position: Three constructions are possible; the simplest is that the offender grieved not the apostle only but, to some extent, the whole church, which was the chief sufferer from the scandal
The qualification refers to the people rather than the degree of grief: only a part of them had caused him pain, so it would be unreasonable to load the rest with that party's blame
Read as one continuous sentence, he has not so much grieved me as, in some measure, all of you; the reading that makes it mean a part of the saints only is more ingenious than solid
He has grieved the apostle only in common with the rest, the parenthesis keeping him from bearing hard on a body that had acted promptly
The majority, by the more, so that the decision had not been unanimous; the minority were either those who resented the apostle's dictation or those who boasted of their freedom
The whole assembled society, since the words cannot naturally describe a single bishop or a bench of elders, though a single early example makes no binding rule
Not the rulers of the church only: the whole congregation acquiesced in the sentence
Better rendered censure or rebuke; a meeting of the church, the man delivered over, possibly some bodily suffering, and almost certainly exclusion from religious and social fellowship
The excommunication of the incestuous person, or the censure laid upon him by the church
Whatever it was, the man has already suffered sufficiently, and the pleading for him is a proof of parental tenderness

outliers.note: Alone turns the refusal to name the offender into a question about church records, asking whether the names of offending brethren should be entered on the books of sessions and presbyteries to be handed down to posterity.

Alone arraigns the ancient bishops by this rule, since where the apostle is satisfied with repentance they issued canons of three years, of seven, and in some cases of a whole lifetime, which either alienate the offender further or teach him hypocrisy.

9.pericope_label: To whom ye forgive any thing, I forgive also, lest Satan get an advantage

schools.summary: On the ninth verse, note first that the tense would not be decisive even if it were the epistolary aorist, so the reference has to be settled from the sense. Two readings are open. The words may mean, I write to you thus to see whether you are as obedient now as you were before, in one line of action as in the other; or, if the first epistle is meant, the directions given there were intended not only for the removal of a scandal and the reformation of the man who caused it, but also as a test of obedience. On the whole the former seems preferable, since it scarcely seems like this writer to make a punishment a trial of obedience; and there is a characteristic subtle delicacy of thought in his suggesting that, having shown obedience in punishing, they should show it also in forgiving. Do not overstate the case either way: obedience was plainly not the only end in view, and nobody was asked to do a wrong thing in order to prove himself; the point is that writing rather than coming in person gave them the opportunity to show themselves willing, and that every object aimed at in the discipline has now been gained. Gloss the noun as proof by testing, a late word which the New Testament has from this writer only, and the adjective obedient as formed from a verb meaning to give ear. On the tenth verse, mark the movement: though absent in body he had made himself a sharer in the censure, and now, anticipating their compliance, he makes himself a sharer in the absolution. Render the verbs as perfects, if I have forgiven; and observe that the case is put hypothetically because he had all but disclaimed the character of an aggrieved person, so that he confines himself to saying, so far as I was aggrieved I have forgiven, and so far as I have forgiven it is for your sake as a body. Then handle the last phrase carefully. It is literally in the face of Christ, so that in the presence of Christ is a possible rendering; trace the noun from the part about the eye, to the face, to the presence. The English is probably right, conveying the same sense as the phrase in the name of our Lord Jesus in the earlier letter, but in a stronger form: he had forgiven as though Christ were acting in him, so that the forgiveness is as authoritative as the censure was, and the authority given to the apostles is claimed here in its fulness. On the eleventh verse, render it literally, lest we should be cheated, or out-manoeuvred, by Satan, from a verb meaning to take advantage of or overreach; and note that the word rendered devices is used especially of evil plans and purposes. Take the metaphor seriously: it is the phraseology of one playing a game against the Tempter in which the souls of men are at once the counters and the stake. The last move had been to give the sinner over with a view to his ultimate deliverance; if the Tempter answers by driving him to despair or recklessness, stratagem must be met by strategy, and the man absolved so that he may be able to resist. Say last that this language comes out of wide experience, from one who had been buffeted by a messenger of Satan, hindered again and again in his work, and always wrestling not with flesh and blood but with principalities and powers.

Read the ninth verse as an answer to an objection they might well have raised, and state the objection first so that the answer has force. What then did you mean, they might say, when you were so indignant because we had not punished him? To be so stern a judge and then all at once a defender, is that not the mark of a man who wavers between conflicting dispositions, unsteady and led by contrary affections? Notice that such a thought might greatly detract from his authority, and give the answer: he has obtained what he asked, and is therefore satisfied, so that he must now give way to compassion. Their carelessness having been corrected, there is nothing left to hinder them from lifting up by their clemency a man now prostrate and downcast. On the tenth verse, show what he does to make the pardon easier for them. He adds his own vote in support of the pardon they extend, as if to say: do not hesitate to forgive; I promise that I shall confirm whatever you have done, and I already subscribe your sentence of forgiveness. Note that he says he does this sincerely and cordially, and that having already shown how much he desired the man's welfare, he now declares that he grants this willingly to them. On the disputed phrase, allow the reading that makes him Christ's lieutenant in the reconciliation, representing his person, and note that some prefer it for that reason; but incline rather to the sense that he forgives sincerely and without any pretence, since this is the phrase he commonly uses to express pure and undisguised rectitude. If the other reading is preferred, observe why the name of Christ is interposed just there: there is nothing that ought to incline us more to the exercise of mercy. On the eleventh verse, distinguish the dangers. It may be referred to what was said about excessive sorrow, since it is a most dangerous fraud of Satan when, depriving us of all consolation, he swallows us up as in a gulf of despair; that is the reading of the Greek father who expounds it so. Prefer, however, to refer it to the apostle and the church together, for the stratagems of Satan beset them in two ways: if they should be excessively harsh and rigorous, or if dissension should arise among them. It very frequently happens that under colour of zeal for discipline a Pharisaical rigour creeps in, which hurries the miserable offender to ruin instead of curing him; but it is rather of the second danger that he speaks, for had the apostle not to some extent favoured their wishes, Satan would have prevailed by kindling strife among them. Then take the closing clause as a standing warning. We know, being warned of it by the Lord, that one stratagem to which he carefully has recourse is this, that when he cannot ruin us by open means he surprises us off our guard by a secret attack. Since we are aware that he assails us by indirect artifices and secret machinations, we must look well before us and take heed that he may not from some quarter do us injury; and since God both warns us that Satan uses every means to impose upon us and shows us by what methods he does it, it is our part to be on the alert, that he may not have a single chink to creep through.

On the ninth verse, keep the sense simple: he has written these things, the advices and commands now given, that he might know whether they are obedient in all things. Do not enlarge it beyond that, and do not let the trial of obedience become the whole point of the discipline. On the tenth verse, show that his sole object in the punishment inflicted upon the transgressor was the man's amendment, and that he therefore promises to ratify, in the name and authority of Christ, the free pardon which he is exhorting them to dispense. Note that he makes no question of their complying with his direction, and observe how mildly he now speaks even of that heinous sin, calling it any thing, once it has been repented of. Then expound the phrase about the person of Christ in the most practical way it will bear, as a rule for the church to copy: as I believe Christ acts toward this penitent soul, so do I; Christ forgives his sin and takes him into favour, therefore let us forgive him his offence against the Church and restore him to its communion. Say also what the phrase implies for the man who pronounces the pardon, that he speaks by the authority with which Christ has invested him, so that the absolution is not a private opinion but a ministerial act. On the eleventh verse, put the danger in its sharpest form. Satan, to whom the man had been delivered, sought to destroy not only his flesh but his soul also; and if one who has given sufficient proof of the sincerity of his repentance is not restored, he may be overwhelmed with sorrow and sink into despair. Then widen it beyond the individual, for the discipline of the Church is on trial as well as the man. If this is how it ends, that discipline will be represented not as emendatory but as leading to destruction; and our enemies would most gladly avail themselves of that, since they wish to discredit the ministry, and there is always at hand a devil to suggest evil and prompt men to do it. Close with the duty that follows: let us be careful to remove, both from Satan and from those who serve him, all the occasions which might turn to the disadvantage or disparagement of the Gospel of Christ. And add the note that gives the whole verse its weight, that the loss of one soul is a common loss, and no church can afford to treat it as the offender's private affair.

debates.question: Which letter is meant by for to this end also did I write?

sides.position: The present letter, written to see whether they are as obedient now as before; it scarcely seems like the apostle to make a punishment a trial of obedience
The earlier one: writing rather than coming in person gave them the opportunity to show themselves willing, and every object aimed at has now been gained
The advices and commands he is giving at this moment

debates.question: What does in the person of Christ mean?

sides.position: More exactly in the presence of Christ, before his face
That rendering is possible, but the English is probably right, a stronger form of the phrase in the name of the Lord Jesus, so that the absolution is as authoritative as the censure
Acting under Christ's eye and accountable to him, after tracing the word from the part about the eye to the face and then to presence
Some prefer the sense that he stood as Christ's lieutenant, but the phrase more probably means that he forgives sincerely and without pretence
As Christ acts toward the penitent soul, so let the church act toward the offender

debates.question: Whose is the danger from Satan's advantage?

sides.position: The offender's, swallowed up in a gulf of despair when deprived of all consolation
Rather the apostle's and the church's, and chiefly the strife that would have been kindled among them had he not met their wishes
The church's discipline itself, brought into contempt or turned into tyranny, so that a member who might have been useful is lost

outliers.note: Alone develops the warning into a sustained figure of a game played against the Tempter, in which the souls of men are at once the counters and the stake, and in which stratagem must be met by strategy.

Alone refers the danger chiefly to dissension within the church rather than to the offender's despair, holding that had the apostle not to some extent favoured their wishes, Satan would have prevailed by kindling strife among them.

themes: that I might know the proof of you, whether ye be obedient in all things
for your sakes forgave I it in the person of Christ
lest Satan should get an advantage of us: for we are not ignorant of his devices

12.pericope_label: When I came to Troas I had no rest in my spirit, and went into Macedonia

schools.summary: Do not pass over the difficulty in these two verses, but state it before answering it, since the reader will feel it whether it is named or not. These words seem on the one hand to be unworthy of the apostle, if because of a brother's absence he threw away so great an opportunity of saving men; and on the other hand they seem to hang apart from the context, coming in where nothing has prepared for them. Ask which of the two should be proved first, and take the second first, for once that is settled the other becomes easier and clearer. To see how they hang upon what precedes, recall what preceded. At the beginning of the letter he said that he would not have them ignorant concerning the affliction which befell him in Asia, that he was weighed down exceedingly, beyond his power. Having then shown the manner of his deliverance, and having inserted the intervening matter, he is of necessity led to teach them that in yet another way he had been afflicted; and the way was this, that he did not find Titus. Once the sequence is seen, the strength of the affliction can be measured. It is fearful indeed, and enough to prostrate the soul, merely to endure trials; but when there is nobody to comfort, and nobody who can help to bear the burden, the tempest becomes greater. That is what was missing at Troas. Then identify the man whose absence weighed so much, for the letter itself supplies the answer further on: Titus is the one whom he afterwards speaks of as having come to him from these very people, of whom he runs through many and great praises, and whom he says he had sent to them. With that in hand, the point of the whole passage appears, and it is not a lapse from duty but an act of love: he tells them these things in order to show that in this matter also he had been afflicted for their sakes. Let the hearer weigh that. The opportunity he left behind him at Troas was left for their sake, and the distress he owns to was distress on their account; so that what looks at first like an apostle's weakness turns out to be the strongest evidence of his attachment to the very church that had been questioning it.

Mark the transition first. The particle is properly adversative, but frequently denotes transition and serves to introduce something else, whether opposite to what precedes or simply continuative; here it continues and explains the statement already made of his deep affection for the church and his interest in its affairs. Observe that the case of the offender came in as a parenthesis, and that the narrative of what passed after the first epistle is now resumed. On the place, say what is known. Troas was a city of Phrygia or Mysia on the Hellespont, on the regular route from Ephesus to Macedonia, and this route was taken because he had resolved not to go to Corinth. The article may perhaps indicate the district rather than the city. A church there had probably been founded by another hand, since the first visit was limited to a few days and there are no traces of preaching then; now he comes for the gospel's sake, and a flourishing community existed some months later. Note also that the historian records two other visits to Troas but not this one. On the open door, compare the same metaphor used of Ephesus in the earlier letter, and again later of another church; it describes what we should call an opportunity for mission work, and there is something of a coincidence in its being used of two different churches within a comparatively short interval. Then state the difficulty of the passage in a single sentence: here was an open door that he could not enter. On the thirteenth verse, take the tense seriously. It is a perfect, a vivid dramatic recital, and should not be flattened into a simple past, for he still feels the shadow of that restlessness as he writes. Gloss the noun as a letting up or release, from a verb meaning to relax, and the participle rendered taking my leave as from an old verb meaning to set apart, which in the later language means to separate oneself from, to bid adieu. Then reconstruct the arrangement that had failed, since the verse assumes it. Instead of coming straight from Ephesus as he had at first intended, or pressing on through Macedonia as he purposed when he wrote the first epistle, he had sent Titus to ascertain what effect that letter had produced, and Titus was to return to him at Troas. Not meeting him there, and in eager anxiety to hear more than had already reached him, he left Troas in spite of the opening it presented and hastened into Macedonia; taking the route he had taken before, he would probably go to Philippi, and we may conjecture without much risk of error that it was there he and Titus met. Note last how rare this is: seldom did he leave an inviting field where there was prospect of signal success in order to go elsewhere. It is adduced here to show his interest in this church; and it also shows that there may be cases in which it is proper for a minister to leave a field of great and inviting usefulness for another.

Read these verses as further confirmation of what has been said about his coming, since by mentioning what he had been doing in the meantime, in what places he had been and what route he had followed, he strengthens the explanation already given. He came to Troas from Ephesus for the sake of the gospel, for he would not have gone in that direction on his way to Achaia had he not wished to pass through Macedonia. Say plainly what happened there. He did not find Titus, whom he had sent to Corinth, and from whom he ought to have learned the state of that Church; and although he might have done much good in Troas, and although an opportunity was presented to him, yet setting everything aside he went to Macedonia, wanting to see Titus. Draw the inference: here is evidence of a singular degree of attachment, that he was so anxious about them that he could settle nowhere, even where a large prospect of usefulness offered, until he had learned the state of their affairs. Hence it appears why he delayed his coming; he did not wish to come until he had first talked with Titus, and he afterwards learned from Titus's report that matters were not yet ripe for such a visit. So he loved them so much that he accommodated all his journeyings and long circuits to their welfare, and came later than he had promised, not because he had rashly changed his plan in forgetfulness of it, nor because he was carried away by levity, but because the delay was more profitable for them. On the open door, give the metaphor its meaning and then its use. It signifies that an opportunity of promoting the gospel had presented itself; a corresponding figure is common in Greek and Latin writers, and the rabbinic writers use the word gate in the same way, as when it is said of the angel's question to Hagar that he knew the answer already but asked in order to give her a gate, an opening, for speaking with him. As an opportunity of entering is furnished when the door is open, so the servants of the Lord make advances when an opportunity is presented, and the door is shut when no prospect of usefulness is held out. Turn that into a rule both ways. When the door is shut it becomes us to enter upon a new course, rather than to weary ourselves to no purpose by useless labour; and where an opportunity of edifying presents itself, let us consider that by the hand of God a door is opened for introducing Christ there, and let us not refuse to employ ourselves in what service we can when we see that God invites us so kindly. Then face the objection honestly, that an open door is itself evidence of a divine call, and that it may therefore seem he erred in leaving unimproved an opportunity placed within his reach, breaking away in another direction after little more than a beginning. Answer it from the strength of the attachment already proved, and let the reader see that a rule about doors does not override the claims of a particular flock upon a particular pastor.

Place the journey first, since the verse assumes a route the reader may not have in mind: this seems to belong to that passage from Asia into Macedonia of which only a short account is given in the history. Say what he found there, and be exact about the opportunity, for it was real. There was free liberty to speak and many were willing to hear; the Lord had opened him a particular door to preach the Gospel, and he says elsewhere how much he rejoices and glories in such an opening. Then say what he did not find. He had written the former letter and had not yet heard what effect it had produced upon their minds, and Titus, who was to have returned with the account, was not there. Give the reason for the restlessness plainly, from the love that lay behind it: he was so concerned for them, through the love he bore them, that he was greatly distressed at not finding Titus returned to give him an account of their state; and his want of rest came from an earnest desire to know how his letter had been received. Then explain the move to Macedonia as a practical step rather than a flight: being much nearer to them there, he might more easily be informed concerning them, and there in fact Titus did come to him and gave a joyous account of their state. Note also where this leaves the reader in the letter, for it matters to the reading of what follows. The thread of the discourse is taken up again several chapters later, and between this point and that there is interposed an admirable digression concerning what he had done and suffered elsewhere, the profit of which he by this means derives to these people also, and which serves as a prelude to his defence against the false apostles. Let the hearer take one lesson from the whole. A door opened by God is not a summons to stay at any cost; the same love that makes a man labour in one place may make him leave it, and the anxiety of a pastor for a people who have been questioning him is itself a kind of testimony they were in no position to demand.

Tell the reader plainly what has happened to the argument, for he will otherwise lose his place. After the directions concerning the excommunicated person the apostle makes a long digression, to give an account of his travels and labours for the furtherance of the gospel and of the success he had in them, declaring at the same time how much he was concerned for these people in their affairs, since he had no rest in his spirit when he did not find Titus at Troas as he expected, from whom he had hoped to understand more perfectly how it fared with them. Note that we find afterwards that when he had come into Macedonia he was comforted by the coming of Titus and by the information he gave concerning them; so that we may look upon all that follows, for several chapters together, as a kind of parenthesis. Then take two observations from the verses themselves. First, his unwearied labour and diligence in his work. He travelled from place to place to preach the gospel, going to Troas and thence into Macedonia, so that he was prevented from passing by Corinth as he had designed; but though he was prevented in his design as to the place of working, he was unwearied in the work itself. Let that distinction stand, for it covers many a frustrated plan: a man may be hindered as to where he shall labour, and not hindered at all as to whether he shall. Second, his success in his work, for a great door was opened to him of the Lord. He had a great deal of work to do wherever he came, and had good success in it, since God made manifest the savour of his knowledge by him in every place where he came. Observe how the two sides of that met. He had an opportunity to open the door of his mouth freely, and God opened the hearts of his hearers, as he opened the heart of Lydia; and neither the freedom of the speaker nor the opening of the hearers is of any use without the other. Let this be matter of thankfulness to God and of rejoicing to the soul, and let the good success of the gospel be reckoned a good reason for a Christian's joy, since it is God who gives both the matter for triumph and the heart to triumph, and to him therefore belongs the praise and glory of it all.

sides.position: With the affliction in Asia named at the opening of the letter: not finding Titus is one more affliction in that series
The case of the offender was the parenthesis, and the narrative of what followed the first epistle is here resumed
This resumed narrative is itself the digression, and runs on for several chapters more
The connecting particle is properly adversative but often merely transitional, and here continues the account of his affection for them

sides.position: The act seems unworthy of him, if for a brother's absence he threw away so great an opportunity of saving men; the answer is that the affliction, and the leaving, were for their sakes

I had no rest in my spirit, because I found not Titus my brother
taking my leave of them, I went from thence into Macedonia

14.pericope_label: God always causeth us to triumph in Christ; a savour of life unto life

schools.summary: Account first for the abruptness of the thanksgiving, which is at first somewhat startling. Its source is not in what has just been written or spoken but in what was passing through the writer's memory: he had met Titus, and that disciple had been as a courier bringing tidings of a victory. Several causes of joy ran together, that Titus had come and removed his distress, that he had learned the letter's directions had been obeyed, and that his own work in Macedonia had signal success; so that being compelled to leave Troas had turned out to be the cause of great joy. Then correct the verb, and be firm about it. There is no authority for the causative meaning given to it in the English version; elsewhere it is rightly translated of leading in triumph, and the true rendering gives a much more characteristic thought. It would be unlike this writer to speak of himself as the triumphant commander of God's army; it is altogether like him to give God the glory and own that He had triumphed, apostle and penitent, faithful and rebellious, alike taking their place in the procession. Note too that no example of the causative use of this late word has been found, and that it belongs to a family in which such a sense would be possible but is not attested. Then unfold the imagery, which is clearly that of the solemn triumphal procession of a Roman general. Point out that the writer had not yet been at Rome, where alone such triumphs were celebrated, and had therefore never seen one, so that he wrote from what he had heard, whether from Roman Jews at Corinth, many of them of the imperial household, or from soldiers he had met at Philippi. He had heard how the conqueror rode along the sacred way in his chariot, followed by troops and prisoners, captive kings and trophies; how fragrant clouds of incense accompanied the march, rising from fixed altars or wafted from censers; and how at the foot of the Capitoline hill some of the prisoners were led off to execution while others were pardoned and set free. Keep that last detail in view, for the next verses turn upon it: some who appeared in the triumph were on their way to deliverance and some on their way to perish, which is the exact force of the words rendered saved and lost. Then take the incense as the figure of the preaching, and note the sterner side of it. Keeping the procession in mind, think of the widely different effect the same odour would have on the two classes of prisoners: to some it would be as a breath from Paradise, giving life and health; to others its sweetness would seem sickly and pestilential, coming as from a charnel house, having in it the savour of death and leading to death as its issue. Say frankly that some people are actually hardened by preaching. Then let the closing question stand as it is meant to. It forces itself upon every true teacher: who can feel qualified for a work which involves such tremendous issues? In himself no one is; and the answer, which the next verses supply, is that God has made us able ministers, and that our sufficiency is of God.

Guard the thanksgiving before expounding it, for the passage is a man's account of his own success and might easily be mistaken. He glories in the fruit of his ministry and shows that he had been far from idle in the places he had visited; but that he may do this in no invidious way he sets out with a thanksgiving. He does not extol his own actions in a spirit of ambition, that his name may be held in renown, nor does he give thanks in mere pretence after the manner of the Pharisee while lifted up with pride; he desires from his heart that whatever is worthy of praise be recognised as the work of God alone. Add the second motive, which is theirs and not his: he recounts his own praises with a view to their advantage, that on hearing how fruitfully he had served the Lord elsewhere they may not allow his labour to be unproductive among themselves, and may learn to respect a ministry which God everywhere rendered glorious. For what God so illustriously honours, it is criminal to despise; and nothing was more injurious to these people than to hold his apostleship and doctrine in low esteem, nothing more advantageous than to hold both in honour. Since he had begun to be held in contempt by many, silence was not his duty; and this holy boasting is set in opposition to the revilings of the wicked. On the verb, take it in the causative sense, as the Hebrew conjugation would give it, so that the meaning is, who maketh us to triumph. Captives are said to be led in triumph when by way of disgrace they are bound with chains and dragged before the conqueror's chariot; but the meaning here is rather that he was a sharer in the triumph enjoyed by God, because it had been gained by his instrumentality, just as the lieutenants of the general rode beside his chariot as sharers in the honour. All the ministers of the gospel fight under God's auspices and procure for him the victory and the honour; and he honours each of them with a share according to the station assigned him and the exertions he has made, so that they enjoy a triumph of their own, though it is God's rather than theirs. Then transfer the metaphor as the text does, from the knowledge of Christ to the persons of the ministers, and for the same reason. They are called the light of the world not because they shine with their own lustre but because they hold forth the torch of the gospel; so they have the name of a sweet savour, not as emitting any fragrance of themselves, but because the doctrine they bring is odoriferous and can imbue the whole world with its fragrance. Note that an allusion to the perfumes censed during the triumphal processions is probable here, an odour which might not improperly be called the odour of death to the vanquished and of life to the conquerors. Then state the hardest part of the passage without softening it. Faithful ministers are a sweet odour before God not merely when they quicken souls by a wholesome savour, but also when they bring destruction to unbelievers; both odours are grateful to God, that by which the elect are refreshed unto salvation and that from which the wicked receive a deadly shock. Draw the consolation out of it. Whatever the issue of our preaching, it is well-pleasing to God if the Gospel is preached, and it does not detract in any degree from the dignity of the Gospel that it does not do good to all; if this is acceptable to God it ought to be so to us, and the heralds of the Gospel who stand in bad odour with the world because their success falls short of their desires have this choice consolation, that what is an offensive smell to the world is a sweet fragrance to God and to angels. On the closing question, some take it as a guard against arrogance, since to discharge the office of a loyal and faithful apostle exceeds all human power; others as a remark upon the small number of good ministers. Prefer to find in it an implied contrast which is expressed shortly afterwards: profession is common and many boast confidently, but to have the reality is a distinguished excellence and very thin sown. He claims nothing for himself but what will be discovered to be in him if trial is made, and by claiming a peculiar excellence he separates himself from the herd of those who had little experience of the Spirit's influence.

Explain what a triumph was before explaining what it means here, because the figure governs three verses and the reader will not follow them otherwise. It was a public and solemn honour conferred by the Romans upon a victorious general by allowing him a magnificent procession through the city, not granted by the senate unless he had gained a signal and decisive victory or conquered a province. The general was clad in a rich purple robe interwoven with figures of gold, his buskins beset with pearls, and he wore a crown at first of laurel and afterwards of pure gold; in one hand a branch of laurel, the emblem of victory, and in the other his truncheon. He was carried in a chariot adorned with ivory and plates of gold, usually drawn by two white horses, his children at his feet or on the chariot horses. To keep him humble amid these honours a slave stood at his back casting out incessant reproaches and carefully enumerating all his vices. Musicians led the procession; then young men leading the victims, their horns gilded and their heads adorned with garlands; then carts loaded with the spoils; then the captive kings and generals loaded with chains; then the triumphal chariot, before which the people strewed flowers and shouted; then the senate, and last the priests with the sacrificial utensils and the white ox. They passed through the triumphal arch along the sacred way to the capitol, where the victims were slain; and during all this time the temples stood open and every altar smoked with offerings and incense. Then bring it home to the readers, for the city of Corinth had reason to know what a triumph was: about two centuries before, the Roman consul had conquered all Achaia and destroyed Corinth, and by order of the senate had a grand triumph and took his surname from the province. The apostle now had a triumph of a widely different kind over the same people; his triumph was in Christ, to whom he gives all the glory, his sacrifice was thanksgiving, and the incense offered on the occasion caused the savour of the knowledge of Christ to be made manifest in every place. Note that to triumph implies not only victory but an open manifestation of it, and that as incense and perfumes were burned near the conqueror, so the writer alludes to the different effects strong perfumes have upon different persons, reviving some while throwing others into violent disorders. Then apply the double effect without flinching, but state the ground of it exactly. Since God has determined that those who believe shall be saved and those who believe not shall perish, the preacher is equally acceptable to him whether he preaches to some who obstinately reject and so perish, or to others who believe and are saved. Cite the old rabbinic sayings, that as the bee brings honey to its owner but stings others, so it is with the words of the law, which were a savour of lives to Israel and a savour of death to the peoples of the world; and note that the meaning of those sayings is as plain as this one. Then be careful how the terms are used. Those who are saved and those who perish mean simply those who receive and obey the gospel and those who reject it and live and die in sin; no other kind of election and reprobation is known in the Book of God, however they may abound in the books of men. Warn against the temper that turns this doctrine into a fence around a favoured few, for the Jews were possessed with such an exalted opinion of their own excellence that they imagined all the mercy of God concentrated among themselves; and when men who are not Jews arrogate all salvation to themselves and prove that the death of Christ shall never avail the greater part of mankind, it is the same error in a worse shape. Close on the closing question by asking who is meant. Is it the false apostle who has been labouring to pervert you, or the men to whom God has given an extraordinary commission and sealed it? And answer it in a line: no man living is sufficient for these things, but by the power of God's Spirit.

17.pericope_label: We are not as many, which corrupt the word of God

schools.summary: Render the opening comparison exactly, for the English understates it: not as many, but as most, as the greater number. There is a ring of sadness in the words. Even then the ways of error were manifold and the way of truth was one; among Judaisers and seekers after Greek wisdom, asserters of licence for liberty and questioners of the resurrection, how few were those who preached the true word of God in its purity. Take the reference to be the false teachers at Corinth, and beyond them all who mingle human philosophy or tradition with the pure word of truth. Then gloss the verb rendered corrupt. It occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and not at all in the Greek Old Testament, and is formed from a noun meaning a huckster, a petty chapman, a retailer, and especially a retailer of wine. Such dealers were notorious, then as now, for diluting their wine with water and compounding it of other substances for the sake of gain, so that of all commodities in trade wine perhaps affords the greatest facilities for dishonest tricks; and it is curious how hucksters generally were suspected of putting the best fruit on the top of the basket. Hence the word comes to mean adulterate. Apply it to those who adulterate the word of God for any purpose, and if the imagery of the triumph is still present, connect it with the sweet savour: our incense at any rate is pure; if it brings death, that is through no fault of ours, for it is not a poisoned perfume. Then name the ways in which the corruption is actually done, since the general charge is useless without them. It is done by attaching a philosophical explanation to the facts of revelation and making the theory as important as the fact; by explaining away the offensive points of revelation with the aid of philosophy; and by forcing the facts of Scripture into agreement with the prevalent notions of the day through a mode of interpretation which fritters away the meaning and can make the text mean anything or nothing at pleasure. Say what has come of it. Of all the evils Christianity has sustained, the worst have been those it received from philosophy and from teachers who corrupted the word of God; the fires of persecution it could meet and still be pure, but when corrupted in this way it has been dimmed in its lustre, paralysed in its aims, and shorn of its power. Note in passing that the old English version rendered the clause with a phrase about chopping and changing with the word of God, an idea important and beautiful, though in this one instance that translator missed the sense. Then take the four clauses that answer the charge, and mark how solemn a view of his relation to God as a preacher they express: of sincerity, unmingled honesty and simplicity of aim; as of God, sent by him, under his control and direction; in the sight of God, as if his eye were always upon us, than which nothing is better fitted to make a man honest; and in Christ, in his name and service. Observe that the first two clauses are half connected and half contrasted, since to have said of sincerity alone would have given too much prominence to what is purely subjective: a man cannot be sure that he is sincere unless he knows that his sincerity was given him by God.

Take the verse as the open contrast with the false apostles, made by way of amplifying what has gone before and with a view to excluding them from the praise just claimed. Let the argument be heard in the first person: it is on good grounds that I speak in honourable terms of my apostleship, for I am not afraid of being convicted of vanity if proof is demanded; but many arrogate the same thing to themselves on false grounds, and will be found to have nothing in common with me. Then make an observation the reader will not expect, and it is the key to the verse. It is not likely that the men reproved here preached openly wicked or false doctrines; the probability is rather that they corrupted the right use of doctrine, for the sake either of gain or of ambition, so as utterly to deprive it of its energy. Support that from the vocabulary. The Greek word is taken from retailers or tavern-keepers, who are accustomed to adulterate their commodities that they may fetch a higher price; a historian says of a certain king that he was a huckster, because he retailed everything; another writer speaks of making peace for money, as the Latins spoke of making war for money; and the Greek version of Isaiah says, thy vintners mix the wine with water. The word properly means a retailer, one who deals at second hand, exactly corresponding to our hucksters. Then distinguish the two ways in which the doctrine of God is corrupted, and be careful to hold both. It is corrupted in a gross way when it is mixed up with falsehood and lies, so as to be no longer the pure and genuine doctrine of God, but something falsely commended under that title. It is corrupted in another way when, although it retains its purity, it is turned hither and thither to please men, and disfigured by unseemly disguises for the sake of hunting after favour. Describe that second kind carefully, since it is the commoner. There will be found some in whose doctrine no impiety can be detected, but who hunt after the applause of the world by making a display of their acuteness and eloquence, or are ambitious of some place, or gape after filthy lucre, or are by some means desirous to rise; and these, nevertheless, corrupt the doctrine itself by wrongfully abusing it and making it subservient to their depraved inclinations. This is what ordinarily happens in the case of all who play with the sacred word of God as with a ball and transform it according to their own convenience; for it must necessarily be that they degenerate from the truth and preach a sort of artificial and spurious Gospel. Then set the contrast in its place. Against that corruption he sets sincerity, which may be taken as referring to the manner of preaching or to the disposition of the mind, and the latter is to be preferred; and against the huckstering of the word he sets a faithful and conscientious dispensation of it, since what he has received from God he delivers to the Church from hand to hand, without keeping back or altering anything on the way.

Begin with the answer to the question just asked, for this verse supplies it: God has made us sufficient for these things by giving us his own pure doctrine, the ministry of reconciliation, which we conscientiously preserve and preach. Then state the contrast, and do not blunt it: we do not act like many among you who, having received that doctrine, corrupt it, mingling with it their own inventions and explaining away its force and influence so as to accommodate it to men of carnal minds. Then open the word, which is the heart of the verse. It signifies acting like an unprincipled vintner, for that class of men have ever been notorious for adulterating their wines, mixing them with liquors of no worth so as to increase the quantity, and then selling the mixture at the price of the pure. The Greek version of Isaiah renders the prophet's charge in exactly this way, thy vintners mix thy wine with water, meaning that the false prophets and corrupt priests adulterate the word of God and render it of none effect by their explanations and traditions. Show that the word covers more than wine. It has been used among both Greeks and Latins to signify a prostitution of what is right and just for the sake of gain, as in the phrases for making peace for money and making war for money; in short, for any artifice employed to make a thing look better than it is, or to mingle what is excellent with what is not, in order to promote the gain of the adulterator. It is used by a comic poet of an old woman patched and painted to hide her deformity, of whom it is said that if the paint were washed off her wrinkled face would plainly appear. Say plainly that the same word covers those who mix bad wine with good and those who patch and mend old clothes for sale, and let the hearer make the application to preaching for himself. Then take the four positive clauses in order and give each its own weight. Of sincerity: we receive the doctrine pure from God, keep it pure, and deliver it in its purity to mankind, without any mixture. From God: this rises higher still, for we transmit his pure word and not our own. In the sight of God: whom we regard as always present and noting every word of our tongue, our whole souls and all their motives being known to him. In Christ: the tongue is ours but the power is God's, and the words are such as he gives, approves and blesses. Close with the comparison that binds the verse together and turns it upon the conscience. As the unprincipled vintner knows that he adulterates the wine, his own conscience testifying it against him, so we know that we deliver the sincere truth of God, our conscience witnessing that we deliver it to you as we received it by the inspiration of the Spirit of truth. Let every man who handles the word ask which of those two consciences is his.

sides.position: Rather most, the greater number, and there is a ring of sadness in it, since the ways of error were manifold and the way of truth one
The false apostles, described by their number, there having been great swarms of false teachers in the earliest times; some copies, with the Syriac and Arabic, read as the rest
The false teachers at Corinth, and beyond them all who mingle human philosophy or tradition with the pure word of truth
Not men who preached openly wicked or false doctrine, but men who corrupted the right use of doctrine for gain or ambition, so as to deprive it of its energy

debates.question: What is the force of the verb rendered corrupt?

sides.position: From the huckster or pedlar, common in every stage of Greek; such men were suspected of laying the best fruit on top of the basket
From the tavern-keeper: an unprincipled vintner mixing wine with worthless liquor to increase the quantity, as the Greek Isaiah says thy vintners mix thy wine with water
Properly a retailer, one who deals at second hand; and by extension any prostitution of what is right for the sake of gain

outliers.note: Alone weighs philosophy against persecution and judges that the worst evils Christianity has sustained came from the former, since the fires of persecution left it pure while philosophy dimmed its lustre and shore it of its power.
Alone illustrates the verb from a comic poet, who used it of an old woman patched and painted to hide her deformity, whose wrinkled face would plainly appear if the paint were washed off.
